headline: Dekiru began as ideku in the Man'yōshū of 759, written 出で来.

sources.quote: /ideku/ → /deku/ → /dekuru/ → /dekiru/

Originally appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE and other Old Japanese texts as 出(い)で来(く) (ideku), as a compound of 出(い)で (ide, “going out”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 出(い)づ (izu, ancient idu, ancient form of modern 出(で)る (deru, “to come out, to go out”))) + 来(く) (ku, “to come”, the ancient form of modern 来(く)る (kuru, “to come”)). The original meaning was “to come out”, extending in figurative contexts to a sense of “to appear, to become manifest”.

Phonologically, ideku shifted to deku by the mid-1400s in the Muromachi period, as the low-tone initial i dropped out, vaguely similar to the way that unstressed syllables in English may disappear. This deku then underwent a common shift in Muromachi Japanese to become dekuru, where all bigrade verbs and irregular verbs underwent a shift that included a -ru on the end of the plain form, in part through a fusion of the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) that has always ended in -ru for these verbs, and the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “terminal form”) that is used at the end of sentences.

As a later part of this same shift, the central vowel shifted from -u- to -i- to produce dekiru, as the main vowel -i- for the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) came to be used for all conjugated forms.

Over this same period, the meaning gradually shifted from “to come out” to include “to appear, to become manifest”, and from there “to come into existence anew”. This then extended further to “to occur, to happen; to be born; to be created, to be produced”, and thence “to come to fruition; to be completed, to be finished (with positive overtones)”. The underlying sense of latent existence gave rise to the meaning of “to be capable of making or producing something”, and then simply “to be able to do”.
In slang contexts in the early 1800s, dekiru came to mean “to have sex”, perhaps similar to the development of the English phrases “to do it, to get some, to get it on”.

headline: Uwasa originally referred to private conversation about one's social superiors, and is possibly from 上 (ufa, “up, upward”).

sources.quote: /ufasa/ → /uwasa/
First attested in works from the Muromachi period.

Considering that the meaning originally referred to private conversation about one's social superiors, possibly derived as a compound of 上 (ufa, “up, upward”, ancient reading of modern uwa, the combining form of modern ue; in reference to those of higher social standing) + さ (sa, “-ness”, suffix indicating state or degree).

headline: Mechakucha's etymology is hypothetical: 無茶 (mucha) shifted to 滅茶 (mecha) by ateji.

sources.quote: This etymology is hypothetical. Since that 無茶 (mucha) shifted to 滅茶 (mecha) by ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), there may be an idea raised that a 滅茶 (mecha) ("ruined tea" or thus, "wrongly prepared tea") would be a 苦茶 (kucha) ("bitter tea"), which would also favor the sense of four-character idioms or 四字熟語 (yojijukugo).

headline: Noseru, “to take on board”, is cognate with 載せる (noseru), from the Classical Japanese verb のす (nosu).

sources.quote: From Classical Japanese verb のす (nosu). Cognate with Japanese 載(の)せる (noseru).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Sakan is a sound shift from 盛り (sakari), sharing a root with 栄える (sakaeru, “to thrive”) and 咲く (saku, “to bloom”).

sources.quote: First attested in the late 11th century.

Sound shift from 盛(さか)り (sakari), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 盛(さか)る (sakaru, “to be in prime condition”), itself sharing a root with 栄(さか)える (sakaeru, “to thrive, to boom”) and 咲(さ)く (saku, “to bloom”).

headline: Saraishū is analyzed as either 再来 (sarai, “two next”) plus 週, or 再 (sa, “again”) plus 来週 (raishū); first attested in 1966.

sources.quote: Analyzed by references as either a compound of 再来 (sarai, “two next, the one after next”) + 週 (shū, “week”), or a compound of 再 (sa, “again, one more”) + 来週 (raishū, “next week”).
First attested in 1966.
